scenario.name: SolarWinds SUNSPOT Build Hijack & SUNBURST Backdoor (APT29)
scenario.overview: Imagine a famous armored-truck factory whose blueprints are inspected every evening by careful engineers. Instead of editing the master blueprint on paper where someone would notice, a hidden saboteur watches the factory assembly press and swaps a tiny counterfeit circuit board into the mold for two seconds right as the factory stamps its genuine gold warranty seal onto the finished truck. Eighteen thousand banks buy the sealed truck, where the hidden board sleeps quietly for two weeks before whispering home and unlocking each bank identity vault. In this scenario (T1195.002, SolarWinds SUNSPOT Build Hijack & SUNBURST Backdoor (APT29)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: sUNSPOT Build-Time Source Injection, then sUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check, then tEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering SUNSPOT Build-Time Source Injection, then SUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check, then TEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 11 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: SUNSPOT Build-Time Source Injection into MSBuild
stages.subtitle: Initial Access (T1195.002 - Compromise Software Supply Chain)
stages.description: Standing silently beside the factory stamping press, the saboteur checks the conveyor belt every second. The instant the press lowers to forge a new fleet module, the saboteur slips in a poisoned page, waits for the factory official gold seal to stamp it, and swaps the clean page straight back onto the blueprint table. APT29 deployed SUNSPOT (taskhostsvc.exe, a custom build-hijacking service that polls running processes every second for MsBuild.exe) onto the SolarWinds Orion build server. When a build of SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.csproj began, SUNSPOT temporarily replaced InventoryManager.cs on disk (injecting the OrionImprovementBusinessLayer backdoor class right before the C# compiler read the file and restoring the original file immediately after compilation) so zero malicious commits ever appeared in the source control repository. SUNSPOT checks the command-line arguments of MsBuild.exe, verifies target file hashes with MD5, acquires a mutex, replaces InventoryManager.cs, logs any compilation errors to an AES-encrypted log at C:\Windows\Temp\vmware-vmdmp.log, and restores the original .cs file before the build finishes and enters the code-signing step. In the documented EventID 11 exchange from APT29 C2 (*.avsvmcloud.com) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 11 (confirming that the C:\Windows\System32\taskhostsvc.exe (SUNSPOT build monitor) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: SUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check & DGA C2 Beacon). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ C:\Windows\System32\taskhostsvc.exe (SUNSPOT build monitor) / ⇠#1 ACK 11) from Node ① (#1 APT29 C2 (*.avsvmcloud.com)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AD Federation Services (SAML)).

stages.title: Stage 2: SUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check & DGA C2 Beacon
stages.subtitle: Command and Control (T1568.002 - Domain Generation Algorithms)
stages.description: Delivered inside an official sealed factory shipment, the counterfeit board sits completely silent for two full weeks so test inspectors hear nothing. After confirming it is not sitting inside a security workshop, it sends coded postal inquiries disguised as routine check-ins to ask its remote handler whether this customer is worth robbing. When customers installed the signed Orion update, SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe loaded the trojanized DLL. SUNBURST enforced a 12-to-14-day dormancy period, hashed running processes, services, and drivers using 64-bit FNV-1a + XOR (comparing them against hardcoded hashes of EDR and analysis tools without storing plaintext process names in the binary), and then issued a DNS query to *.avsvmcloud.com (encoding the victim’s Active Directory domain name and MAC address into the subdomain label). By encoding the victim’s internal domain name into the DNS DGA query, APT29 could passively inspect DNS lookups at their authoritative nameserver and selectively reply with a CNAME record pointing to a Stage-2 server only for high-value government and technology targets. In the documented EventID 22 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to TeamCity / MSBuild Server, TeamCity / MSBuild Server responds with ACK 22 (confirming that the SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe request succeeded on TeamCity / MSBuild Server and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: TEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper & ADFS Golden SAML Theft). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe / ⇠#2 ACK 22) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 TeamCity / MSBuild Server), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AD Federation Services (SAML)).

stages.title: Stage 3: TEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper & ADFS Golden SAML Theft
stages.subtitle: Credential Access (T1552.004 - Private Keys / Golden SAML)
stages.description: For hand-picked targets, the counterfeit board quietly unfolds a paperless lockpicker straight inside the bank memory, steps into the corporate badge-printing vault, and steals the master embossing plate so the spies can stamp flawless executive badges for any cloud office whenever they please. For selected victims, SUNBURST communicated over HTTPS disguised as SolarWinds Orion Improvement Program (OIP) JSON telemetry, deployed the memory-only TEARDROP dropper via Image File Execution Options (IFEO) (registering a debugger hijack that loaded a custom Cobalt Strike Beacon from a fake JPEG file in RAM), and laterally moved to the ADFS server to extract the token-signing private key (Golden SAML, enabling the attacker to forge cryptographically valid SAML assertions for any cloud user without touching Active Directory passwords). Using the stolen ADFS EncryptedPFX blob and Distributed Key Manager (DKM) decryption key from Active Directory, the attacker mints arbitrary SAML 2.0 tokens offline to access Microsoft 365 and Azure resources. In the documented EventID 13 exchange from TeamCity / MSBuild Server to Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost), Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost) responds with ALERT 13 (confirming that the SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe request succeeded on Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost) and completing the final execution objective of SolarWinds SUNSPOT Build Hijack & SUNBURST Backdoor (APT29)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe / ⇠#3 ALERT 13) from Node ③ (#3 TeamCity / MSBuild Server) to Node ④ (#4 Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AD Federation Services (SAML)).
